text: The leather of the steering wheel was cold beneath my palms,
but where my knuckles locked against the rim,
the skin had gone chalk white.
Outside, Route 9 was dissolving into black glass.
November rain fell in thick, greasy sheets,
beating against the windshield with the rhythm of a failing heart.
The wipers scraped back and forth across the glass,
dragging arcs of road grit and yellow glare from oncoming semi-trucks,
but nothing could wipe clean what was glowing on the phone wedged
into my center console.
The screen stayed awake, fed by a cigarette lighter charger cord
that coiled across the gearshift like a thin black viper.
Tomorrow night, the corner suite at the Belvedere.
Do not let your little Sicilian princess smell the bourbon on you.
The sender was saved under the neat clinical label.
Dr. C. Sterling.
Six months.
184 days of archived messages, timestamps,
hotel room reservations booked under corporate medical consultation codes
and voice memos where Camilla Sterling laughed,
low, breathless, and sharp as surgical steel.
In one recording, sent three weeks ago,
while I was attending my cousin Matteo’s wake in South Brooklyn,
she had whispered into the microphone,
"Tell me you don't touch her anymore, Julian.
Tell me her father's ghosts don't crawl into bed between you."
And Julian had replied,
"I haven't touched Francesca in two years without washing my hands
first."
I looked up into the rearview mirror.
The woman looking back at me had dark sunken hollows under her eyes.
Her lips painted the dark garnet red my father used to favor on his
hand-rolled cigars.
There was no grief on her face.
Only a strange petrified stillness.
The kind of silence that settles into the walls of a funeral parlor
after the mourners take their coats and leave the corpse alone with
the tapers.
My husband was a creature of absolute precision.
Julian Vance was the prize horse my father,
Don Lorenzo Moretti, had bought off the Red Hook docks when Julian was
18 years old,
a boy with blood on his shirt and a photographic memory for human
anatomy.
